title: FLORA CITY COUNCIL MEETS
full_story:
The Flora City Council met on Monday afternoon and quickly went through their agenda.

Mayor Linda Spicer called the meeting to order and then opened the floor to public comment.  Cat Osterholtz with C.A.T.S., or Clip and Tip Strays briefly addressed commissioners about their effort to help reduce the feral and stray cat population in Flora and Clay County.  They participate in TNR, or Trap, Neuter and Return, which reduces the overpopulation of cats over the long term by sterilization of feral and stray cats.  Osterholtz states that they are now recognized as a 501(c)(3) non-profit organization.  Since they started working on the issue in November, they have spayed or neutered 120 cats at a rate of 20 per day on the 2nd Tuesday of each month.  Osterholtz says they hope to double the number of animals in the months ahead.  She says they pay $60 to neuter males and $80 to spay females and also offer rabies shots to the animals they treat.  Mayor Spicer thanked Osterholtz for the update and wished them well in their work.

Next, Commissioners approved the meeting agenda and consent agenda.  The latter included approval of past meeting minutes, the Warrant List, and the February Police Activity Report, Building and Zoning Report and Treasurers Report.

In regular business, Mayor Linda Spicer spoke briefly about attending the meeting that Heather Greenwood spoke about at the January Flora City Council meeting put on by Partners for Progress.  The group works with individuals who may have contact with law enforcement but are not in the system.  They seek to deflect these people from further engagement with the legal system by engagement and with the help of behavioral and mental health specialists.  Spicer says the meeting in Flora on March 3rd was well attended.  Changing gears, the mayor also touched on the Pickle Ball Courts and said while people are playing right now, they encourage people to clean up after themselves and not leave trash behind which makes it look bad.

When Mayor Spicer polled commissioners for comment, Phil Wiley offered condolences to the family Mike Bridges, who passed away on March 3.  He was an engineer with Charleston Engineering in Olney and worked on hundreds of local projects around Flora, Clay County and around southeastern Illinois over several decades.  He added that Bridges will be sorely missed.  Wiley then moved on to Flora’s July 4th activities celebrating America’s 250th Birthday.  He adds that it will be a celebration to remember and Flora will be the place to be.

Flora Police Chief Jeremy Ruger presented an ordinance to amend Title 6, Chapter 5, Section 4, to update the police dealing with Inoperable Vehicles Declared To Be A Nuisance.  Commissioners approved the ordinance unanimously.

Flora City Administrator/Economic Development Director Mike Stanford presented four items for council consideration.  First, was an ordinance to annex real estate into the City of Flora owned by Tad and Deandra Thompson on North Worthey Street.  Commissioners approved the measure without dissent.  Next was an ordinance to approve a joint funding agreement for the Safe Routes to School program, which seeks to add 2.5 miles of sidewalks in Flora to make traveling to school safer for local students.  Commissioners approved the $400,000 agreement unanimously. The Council then approved an ordinance seeking grant funding from the Illinois Department of Natural Resources for playground equipment additions to Rotary Park (formerly Kiwanis Park) in the amount of $344,800.  Stanford’s final item of the meeting was an ordinance approving the bid and sale of real estate for 404 West 5th Street to Matt and Amanda Winterrowd in the amount of $800.  Before the meeting ended, Stanford had one informational item.  He stated that the City of Flora has applied for a federal grant for its proposed Wastewater Treat Plant in the amount of $2.5 Million, which he hopes will be approved.

title: MITIGATION PLANNING COMMITTEE MEETING
full_story:
The Clay County Hazard Mitigation Planning Committee will hold its first meeting tomorrow at 1:00 PM.  The meeting will be at the Clay County Health Department and is open to the public.

Clay County will update its hazard mitigation plan to reduce the damages caused by severe weather such as thunderstorms, floods, snow and ice storms, and tornados, among other events.  This plan and the process to update it will be funded through a grant from the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA).

“The Plan describes the natural hazard events that have impacted the County and identifies activities and projects to reduce the risk to our residents and infrastructure,” said Steve Lewis, Flora-Clay County Emergency Services and Disaster Agency Coordinator.  “By having an updated hazard mitigation plan, the County and its participating jurisdictions will remain eligible for federal funds to carry out these projects and activities,” he added.

The Planning Committee includes representatives from the County, their municipalities, townships, school districts, fire protection districts, and healthcare services, as well as technical partners and other stakeholders.  Meetings of this committee will be conducted over the next year as working sessions so that any interested residents can attend and ask questions.  The purpose of these working sessions is to gather and discuss information that will be used to update the Plan.

Lewis added, “This mitigation plan is different from our County’s emergency response plan because it focuses on ways to reduce and prevent damages before they occur.”

title: WEATHER SPOTTER TRAINING
full_story:
The National Weather Service is offering their annual severe weather spotter training on Thursday, at 6:00 pm.  The class will be held at Frontier Community College.

Severe storm spotters are a VITAL part of the severe weather warning process.  Spotters provide critical, and potentially, lifesaving information to their communities and surrounding locations – and to National Weather Service (NWS) forecasters who are using these reports to help issue warnings and keep the public updated during severe weather events.

The in-person training covers severe weather hazards including thunderstorms and tornadoes, safety concerns, planning for and anticipating severe thunderstorms, general storm structure and movement, and identification of important storm features.

This year’s program offers more interactive portions of the sessions.  The session will last about 2 hours and are free and open to the public.  Registration is required and is available at wewather.gov/pah/spottertraining or scan the QR Code on the event flyers.

title: ONLY 1 IN 6 HAVE RACES
full_story:
Only about 17% of the possible primary elections in Illinois are contested this year, illustrating the importance of giving voters more choices.

Illinois has 181 open state and federal seats this year, the vast majority of those in the state General Assembly.  Of the 362 possible primaries, only 61 are contested, split evenly between Democrats and Republicans.  In 2024 nearly nine out of every 10 Republican and Democratic primaries for Illinois state and federal offices were uncontested.

This year in the Illinois General Assembly, only 10.5% of primaries involve competing candidates.  Increasing competition by giving Illinois voters options could increase turnout and lead lawmakers to vote more in line with their constituents’ interests.  It could also be an important step in reversing Illinois’ culture of political corruption.

Research shows that more choice drives voter participation and makes legislators less susceptible to the influence of lobbyists and special interests.  Lightly contested elections also tend to skew policies in favor of powerful special interests.

Illinois should consider reforms that will give voters more choices at the ballot box, such as making it easier for independents to enter the general election like they do in Iowa, Wisconsin and Tennessee.  Until that happens, Illinois will continue to see elections with too few choices and too much influence handed to those already in power.
